scene: Child: (holding a smartwatch, looking at tablet, not paying attention)
Parent: "[inaudible 00:00:00] And then we can start."
Child: (looking at the tablet)
Parent: "Okay, great. So now it's time to start. Which story do you want to pick?"
Child: (pointing at the tablet)
Parent: "And also click the corners to go to the next page or to previous page."
Child: (listening, looking at the tablet)
Parent: "And it's encouraged that you ask questions to your child or your child ask questions to you or to even have a dialogue around the context of the story."
Child: (still looking at the tablet)
Parent: "Okay."
(Note: If there's any audible dialogue from the child that is crucial for context or needed to complete further interaction, it's implied based on the discussion topic.)
Child: (points to the tablet screen)
Parent: How do you go to more pages? I mean, more books?
Child: (places hand on chest and looks at the parent)
Parent: These are the books, right? There's no more?
Child: (nods)
Parent: Yeah.
Child: (continues looking at the parent)
Parent: So you got to pick one of these.
Child: Okay.
Child: (sitting at the table, looking at the parent)
Parent: "First page."
Child: (looking at the tablet)
Child: (sitting at the table, looking down at the tablet)
Parent: "Oh, okay."
Child: (sitting at the table, continuing to look at the tablet)

Parent: "One winter morning, Peter woke up and looked out the window. Snow had fallen during the night. It covered everything as far as he could see. After breakfast, he put on his snowsuit and ran outside. Snow was piled up very high along the street to make a path for walking."
Child: (listening and looking at the tablet)
Child: (looking at the tablet, hands on table)
Parent: Go ahead.

Child: (starts reading aloud) Crunch, crunch, crunch. His feet sank into the snow. He walked with his toes pointing out like this. He walked with his toe pointing in, like that. Then he dragged his feet slowly to make tracks. And he found something sticking out of the snow that made a new track. It was a stick. A stick that was just right for smacking a snow-covered tree. And down fell the snow. Plop on top of Peter's head.

Child: (continues reading aloud) He thought it would be fun to join the big boys in their snowball fight, but he knew he wasn't old enough. Not yet. So he made a smiling snowman and he made angels. He pretended he was a mountain climber. He climbed up a great big tall heaping mountain of snow and slid all the way down. He picked up a handful of snow and another and still another. He packed it round and firm and put the snowball in his pocket for tomorrow. Then he went in his warm house.
Child: (continues reading aloud) He
Child: (sitting at the table, looking at the tablet)
Parent: (sitting at the table next to the child, looking at the tablet) "Sad."
Child: (still looking at the tablet, hands resting on the cheeks)
Parent: (glancing at the child, then back at the tablet) "Sad."
Child: (continues to look at the tablet, hands on the cheeks)
Parent: (smiling, looking encouragingly at the child) "Sad."
Child: (focused on the tablet, listening attentively)

Parent: (reading in an animated tone) "While he slept, he dreamed that the sun had melted all the snow away. Then when he woke up, his dream was gone. Snow was still everywhere. New snow was falling. After breakfast, he called to his friend from across the hall and they went out together into this deep, deep snow."
Child: (pointing to the tablet and smiling)
Parent: (smiling back at the child) "And that's it."
Child: (looking at the tablet, appears thoughtful)
Parent: Bookshelf, I guess. Bookshelf. Okay. Go to a second story, I guess.
Child: (tilts head slightly, still looking at the tablet)
Child: (glancing up at the parent, then back at the tablet)
Parent: Do I have to read them all?
Child: (seems hesitant, slightly frowning)
Child: (appears slightly confused, looking at the tablet)
Parent: Read for about 20 minutes.
Child: (nodding slowly)
Child: (hand on chin, contemplating)
Parent: Okay.
Child: Okay.
Child: (hand still on chin, nodding)
Parent: Okay.
Child: Okay.
Child: (looking at the tablet screen, engaged)
Parent: "The Little Engine that Could."
Child: (still looking at the tablet screen, engaged)

Parent: "Chug. Chug. Chug. Puff. Puff. Puff. Ding dong. Ding dong. The little train rumbled over the tracks. She was a happy little train for she had such a jolly load to carry. Her cars were filled full of good things for boys and girls."
Child: (continuing to look at the tablet screen)

Parent: "There were toy animals. Giraffes, with long necks. Teddy bears, with almost no necks at all. [crosstalk 00:05:11] and even a baby elephant. Then there were dolls. Dolls with blue eyes and yellow curls. Dolls with brown eyes and brown bobbed heads and the funniest little toy clown you've ever saw."
Child: (looking up briefly and pointing at the screen, then back to the tablet)

Parent: "And there were cars full of toy engines. Airplanes, tops, jack knives, picture puzzles, books and every kind of thing boy or girl could want. But that was not all. Some of the cars were filled all sorts of good things for boys and girls to eat. Big golden oranges, red sheet apples, bottles of creamy milk for their breakfast, fresh spinach for their dinners, peppermint drops and lollipops for after [inaudible 00:06:17]."
Child: (looking back at the tablet screen, still engaged)
Parent: "The little train was carrying all these wonderful things to the little boys and girls on the other side of the mountain. She puffed along merrily."
Child: (looking at hand with concern)
Parent: What's wrong? You okay?
Child: (shows hand to parent)
Parent: Is it pinching you?
Child: (shakes head and looks at parent)
Parent: Don't reach in there like that.
Child: (rests elbows on table and places chin in hands)
Parent: Okay.
Child: (nods and looks at the tablet)
Child: (looking intently at the tablet, hands near chin)

Parent: "Then all of a sudden she stopped with a jerk. She simply could not go another inch. She tried and she tried but her wheels would not turn. What were all those good little boys and girls on the other side of the mountain going to do without the wonderful toys to play with and the good food to eat?"
Child: (still looking at the tablet, hands near chin)
Parent: "Here comes a shiny new engine," said the funny little clown who jumped out of the train. "Let's ask him to help us."
Child: (continues to look at the tablet, hands near chin)

Parent: "So all the dolls and toys cried out together. 'Please shiny new engine. Won't you please pull our train over the mountain. Our engine has broken down and the good boys and girls on the other side won't have any toys to play with or good food to eat unless you help us.'"
Child: (focused on the tablet, hands still near chin)

Parent: "But the shiny new engine snorted. 'I pull you? I'm no passenger engine. I have just carried a fine, big train over the mountain with more cars than you've ever dreamed of. My train had sleeping cars, comfortable [inaudible 00:07:58] and dining carts where waiters bring whatever hungry people want to eat. The parlor cars in which people sit in, soft arm chairs and look out of big plate glass windows. I pull the likes of you, indeed not!'"
Child: (pointing to the tablet with one hand, looking at parent)
Parent: That's so mean.
Child: (looking at the tablet, appears engaged)
Parent: That is so mean, right?
Child: (still looking at the tablet, appears attentive and thinking)
Child: (pointing at the tablet screen, looking at the tablet closely)

Parent: And off he steamed to the roundhouse where engines live when they are not busy. How sad the little train and all the dolls and toys felt. Then the little clown called out, "The passenger engine is not the only one in the world. Here is another engine coming. A great big strong one. Let us ask him to help us."
Child: (nods slightly, continues to engage with the tablet)
Child: (still pointing at the tablet, listening closely)
Parent: The little toy clown moved his flag and the big strong engine came to a stop.
Child: (leans on her hand, continues to look at the tablet)
Child: (taps on the screen)
Parent: He looks [inaudible 00:09:01]
Child: (continues to interact with the tablet)
Child: (pointing at the tablet, looking at it)
Parent: Yeah, right?
Child: (pointing at the tablet, looking at it)
Parent: Yeah.
Child: (pointing at the tablet, looking at it while resting head on hand)

Parent: "Please, oh please, big engine", cried all the dolls and toys together. "Won't you please pull our train over the mountain? Our engine has broken down and the good little boys and girls on the other side won't have any toys to play with or good food to eat unless you help us." But the big strong engine billowed, "I'm a freight engine. I've just pulled a big train loaded with big machines over the mountain. These machines print books and papers for grownups to read. I'm a very important engine, indeed. I won't pull the likes of you."
Child: (pointing at the tablet, looking at it)

Parent: And the freight engine puffed off indigently to the roundhouse. The little train and all the dolls and the toys were very sad. "Cheer up!" Cried the little toy clown. "The freight engine is not the only one in world. Here comes another. He looks very old and tired. But our train is so little perhaps he can help us."
Child: (pointing at the tablet, looking at it)

Parent: So the little toy waved his flag and [inaudible 00:10:15] the rusty old engine stopped. "Please king engine," cried all the dolls and the toys together. "Won't you please pull our train over the mountain? Our engine has broken down and the boys and girls on the other side won't have any toys to play with or good food to eat unless you help us."
Child: (sitting next to the parent, looking at the tablet)

Parent: "But the rusty old engine said "I'm so tired. I must rest my weary wheels. I can not pull even so a little train as yours over the mountain. I can not, I can not, I can not." And off her rumbled to the roundhouse, chugging "I can not, I can not, I can not.""
Child: (continuing to look at the tablet)
Parent: "Then indeed the little train was very, very sad and the dolls and the toys were ready to cry."
Child: (still looking at the tablet, listening)
Parent: "But they didn't."
Child: (focused on the tablet)
Parent: "The little clown called out, "Here is another engine coming! A little blue engine, a very little one. Maybe she will help us.""
Child: (slightly moving but still attentive to the tablet)
Parent: "The very little engine came chug chugging merrily along when she saw the toy clown's flag. She stopped quickly. "What is the matter, my friends?" She asked kindly."
Child: (leaning in, looking closely at the tablet)

Parent: "Oh little blue engine," cried the dolls and the toys. "Will you pull us over the mountain? Our engine has broken down and the good boys and the girls on the other side won't have any toys to play with or good food to eat unless you help us. Please help. Please help us, little blue engine."
Child: (still looking at the tablet)
Parent: "I'm not very big," said the little engine. "They use me only for switching trains in the yard. I have never been over the mountain."
Child: (looking focused, hands under chin)

Parent: "But we must get over the mountain before the children awake." Said all the dolls and the toys. The very little engine looked up and saw the tears in the dolls eyes and then when she thought of the good little boys and girls on the other side of the mountain who would not have any toys or good food unless she helped. Then she said, "I think I can. I think I can. I think I can." Then she hitched herself to the little train.
Child: (still focused, hands under chin)
Parent: She tugged and pulled and pulled and tugged and slowly, slowly, slowly they started off. The toy clown jumped aboard and all the dolls and the toy animals began to smile and cheer.
Child: (smiling, looking at wristband)
Parent: Yay.
Child: (cheerfully) Yay.
Child: (gesticulating and possibly mimicking the engine sounds while looking at the tablet)

Parent: "Puff, puff. Chug, chug. Went the little blue engine. I think I can. I think I can. I think I can. I think I can. I think I can. I think I can. I think I can. I think I can. I think I can. I think I can."
Child: (smiling and looking at the tablet)
Child: (pointing at the tablet and looking at the parent)
Parent: "Are you done?"
Child: (nodding and looking back at the tablet)
Parent: "Yup, done."
Child: (looking at the tablet and listening attentively)

Parent: "Up, up, up. Faster and faster and faster and faster the little engine climbed. Until at last they've reached the top of the mountain. Down in the valley lay the city. 'Hooray! Hooray!' cried the funny little clown and all the dolls and the toys. 'Good little boys and girls in the city will be happy because you helped us climb, little blue engine.' "
Child: (smiling and possibly repeating the word "Hooray!")
Child: (laughing and looking at the parent)
Parent: "Angel."
Child: (giggles)
Child: (looking at the tablet)

Parent: "And the little blue engine smiled and [inaudible 00:14:04] as she puffed steadily down the mountain. 'I thought I could. I thought I could. I thought I could. I thought I could. I thought I could.'"
Child: (glancing up at the parent, then back at the tablet)
Parent: "I think that's it."
Child: (continues to look at the tablet)
Parent: "Bookshelf. [inaudible 00:14:26] Oh yeah. [inaudible 00:14:28]"
Child: (still focused on the tablet)
Parent: "[inaudible 00:14:30] our short stories."
Child: (slightly shifts position, still engaged with the tablet)
Parent: "The Little House."
Child: (leaning on the chair, looking at the tablet)
Parent: "The Little House."
Child: (listening to the parent, still looking at the tablet)
Parent: "We can [inaudible 00:14:37] for short stories."
Child: (glancing at the parent)
Parent: "Do you want to read The Little House?"
Child: "No."
Parent: "What do you want to read?"
Child: (thinking, looking at the parent)
Child: (Listening and looking at the parent)
Parent: "Short story."
Child: (Looking at the parent)
Parent: "What do you want me to read?"
Child: (Looking at the tablet, appears to be thinking)
Parent: "Short story. [inaudible 00:14:51]"
Child: (Points at the tablet)
Parent: "Short story, all right. Short stories. Those are it. Oh no, there's more."
Child: (Looking intently at the tablet)

Parent: "Once there was a boy named Nikki who wanted his new mittens made from wool as white as snow. [inaudible 00:15:31] At first his [crosstalk 00:15:33] grandmother, Bubba, did not want to knit white mittens. If you drop one in the snow, you'll never find it."
Child: (looking at the tablet and listening to the parent)
Parent: "I'm sure he will."
Child: (continues to look at the tablet, both hands supporting the head, focused on the story)

Parent: "But Nikki wanted snow white mittens. Finally Bubba made them. After she finished, she said 'When you come home, first I will look to see if you're safe and sound. But then I will look to see if you still have your snow white mittens.'"
Child: (points at the tablet screen, seemingly engaged and following along with the story)

Parent: "So off Nikki went and it wasn't long until one of his new mittens dropped in the snow and it was left behind. A mole tired from tunneling along discovered the mitten and burrowed inside. It was cozy and warm and just the right size so he decided to stay. A snowshoe..."
Child: (points at the screen while looking at the tablet, engaged)
Parent: "Hare."
Child: (continues to look at the tablet and follows the story, points at the screen)
Parent: "A snowshoe rabbit came hopping out..."
Child: (turned around, not looking at the parent or the book)

Parent: Hopping by. He stopped for a moment to admire his winter coat. It was then that he saw the mitten and he wiggled in. [crosstalk 00:17:11] At first the mole didn't think there was room for both of them but when he saw the rabbit's big kickers he moved over.
Child: (continues looking away)

Parent: Next a hedgehog snuffling along. Having spent the day looking under leaves for things to eat, he decided to move into the mitten and warm himself. The mole and the rabbit were bumped and jolsted but not being one to argue with someone covered with prickles, they made room.
Child: (turns attention back to the tablet, engaging with the story)
Parent: As soon as the hedgehog disappeared in the mitten, a big owl attracted by the commotion swooped down. When he decided to move in also...
Child: (leans forward, staying focused on the tablet)
Parent: The great horned owl.
Child: (quizzical look) The great horned owl? It doesn't say that.
Child: (looking at the tablet, listening intently)
Parent: "But it is."
Child: (still looking at the tablet, nods slightly)
Parent: "Okay."
Child: (continuing to look at the tablet, pointing with her finger)

Parent: "Decided to move in also, the mole, the rabbit, and the hedgehog grumbled. But when they saw the owl's glinty talons they quickly let him in. Up through the snow appeared a badger. He eyed the mitten and began to climb in."
Child: (points at the badger on the tablet)

Parent: "The mole, the rabbit, the hedgehog and the owl were not pleased. There was no room left. But when they saw his diggers they gave him the thumb. It started snowing but the animals were snug in the mitten."
Child: (smiling, still pointing at the characters on the tablet)
Parent: "A waft of warm steam rose in the air and a fox..."
Child: (leans in closer to the tablet)
Parent: "Fox [inaudible 00:18:32]. A fox trotting by stopping to investigate. Just the sight of the cozy mitten made him feel drowsy. The fox poked his muzzle in."
Child: (seeming excited, points enthusiastically at the fox on the tablet)
Parent: "When the mole, the rabbit, the hedgehog, the owl and the badger saw his shiny teeth, they gave the fox lots of room."
Child: (points to a spot on the tablet, indicating interest)
Parent: (leans in to look at where the child is pointing) "Read it there."
Child: (looks at parent, seemingly confused) "What?"
Parent: (repeats to make it clearer) "Read it there."
Child: (responds to affirmation, looks back at the tablet) "Read it there? I am reading it there."

Parent: (acknowledges child's confirmation, starts reading the next part of the story) "A great bear lumbered by. He spied the mitten all lumped up but not being one to be left out in the cold, he began to nose his way in. The animals were packed in as tightly as can be but what animal would argue with a bear."
Child: (looking at the tablet, sitting close to the parent with their arms around a cushion)
Parent: "Because he can kill you."
Child: (nods and moves slightly closer to the tablet)
Parent: "Yup."
Child: (keeping their gaze on the tablet, still holding the cushion)

Parent: "The mitten swelled and stretched. It was pulled and bulged to many times its size but Bubba's knitting held fast. Along came a meadow mouse, no bigger than an acorn. She wriggled into the one space left and made herself comfortable on top of the great bear's nose."
Child: (pointing at the tablet screen, continues to look intently at it)
Parent: "Uh oh."
Child: (points again, looking interested)
Parent: "The bear tickled by the mouse's whiskers gave an enormous sneeze."
Child: (continues to point at the tablet, looking at the text or images on the screen)
Parent: (stays close to the child, looking at the screen as well)
Child: (looking at the tablet and pointing)
Parent: "Achoo!" The force of the sneeze shot the mitten up into the sky.
Child: (looking at the tablet, holding a plush toy)
Parent: Achoo.
Child: (looking at the tablet, holding a plush toy)

Parent: And scattered animals in all directions. On his way home, Nikki saw a white shape in the distance. It was the lost mitten silhouetted against the blue sky. As he ran to catch his snow white mitten, he saw Bubba's face in the window. First, she looked to see if he was safe and sound. And then she saw that he still had his new mitten.
Child: (leaning forward, pointing at the tablet)
Parent: Just a little stretched out, huh?
Child: (waving hand, looking at the tablet)
Parent: Bookshelf. Bookshelf.
Child: (pointing at the tablet screen and looking intently at it)
Parent: "Is it [inaudible 00:20:56]"
Child: (nodding slightly, still focused on the tablet)
Parent: "I think so."
Child: (continuing to look at the screen and point at something)
Parent: "Okay."
